title: Ultra-long-context KV/batching/quantization deep dive - Nimbus DX
summary: Deep technical session about supporting ultra long-context workloads (100k-200k tokens). Covered KV cache strategies, hierarchical chunking, batching tradeoffs, quantization approaches for 4-bit/8-bit, runtime kernel choices, and on-prem/VPC constraints. Agreed to run two bench sets (hosted + on-prem) and to share quant profile + kernel logs.
next_steps: Redwood: run hosted 128k benchmark with Nimbus sample dataset and return logs (p95/p99 + GPU metrics)
Nimbus: provide redacted sample documents (10GB) and target prompt patterns by 2025-11-14
Schedule on-prem pilot kickoff w/ infra team for week of 2025-11-24
action_items: Jordan Blake - send benchmark spreadsheet + cost estimate - 2025-11-14
Priya Menon - share per-kernel timing and recommended quant profiles (GPTQ/AWQ notes) - 2025-11-15
Samir Patel - provide sanitized 10GB corpus and typical prompt templates - 2025-11-14
transcript:
[00:00] Jordan Blake: Alright hey everyone thanks for carving time out, um this is Jordan from Redwood, with Priya our SE. How's Nimbus DX doing?
[00:06] Samir Patel: Doing well thanks, busy with the clinical notes ingestion project so excited to dig into the long context stuff.
[00:12] Elena Rossi: Hi all. We flagged this as a hard requirement—we need consistent performance at 100k+ context for multi-document summarization.
[00:18] Priya Menon: Great, that's exactly what we want to go deep on today. We'll go through runtime considerations, KV cache behavior with huge prefixes, batching, and quantization tradeoffs. We'll also call out on-prem/VPC caveats.
[00:29] Marcus Lee: Quick logistics question: will you be able to run any on-prem tests or do we need to provide hardware?
[00:33] Jordan Blake: We can run hosted benchmarks first using your sample set; for on-prem we can support a pilot but we'll need access to your nodes or we can ship an engineer. We'll scope that after the hosted baseline.
[00:42] Samir Patel: Cool.
[00:44] Priya Menon: Okay diving in—big picture: 128k+ token sequences change the cost/latency profile in two ways: attention computation grows roughly quadratically in naive implementations, and KV cache growth affects memory and IO for the past key/values. So we optimize across three axes: algorithmic attention optimizations (e.g., FlashAttention variants, grouped-query attention), memory layout and KV sharding (distributed K/V across GPUs or host offload), and quantization/offloading to reduce memory and improve kernel throughput.
[01:12] Elena Rossi: For us, p95 latency is less critical than throughput for batch jobs, but interactive review tooling still wants sub-second partial outputs for short responses while long summaries can be minutes. So a hybrid latency SLO.
[01:26] Priya Menon: That's a common pattern. Redwood runtime supports continuous streaming so you can surface partials while a long job continues. For batching, we have workload-aware batching: small low-latency requests can bypass batching or go to low-latency pool; large long-context runs route to high-throughput nodes.
[01:44] Marcus Lee: On the KV side we're concerned about eviction and warmup costs. If we cache tens of thousands of tokens per session, evictions could thrash.
[01:51] Priya Menon: Right. Two patterns we've seen: prefix caching for repeated prefixes (e.g., identical system prompts + doc preamble) and hierarchical chunk caching where you cache chunks at multiple granularities. For ultra-long, we recommend chunking source documents into 8k-16k overlapping windows, maintain a chunk-index, and keep hot-chunks pinned in GPU-resident KV with LRU + TTL. Less-hot chunks can be offloaded to host memory or NVMe.
[02:17] Samir Patel: Offloading to host memory—what's the perf hit?
[02:20] Priya Menon: Depends on interconnect. On a single node with PCIe gen4 and pinned host memory, we'd see a 2-4x throughput penalty for KV lookups vs GPU-resident. If you're on RDMA between nodes, and we've got NVMe local cache with asynchronous prefetching, the effective hit can be reduced because we prefetch the next N chunks based on access pattern predictions.
[02:41] Elena Rossi: What's the practical RAM and GPU requirement to do 128k with 7B/13B vs 70B models?
[02:48] Priya Menon: For quantized 7B/13B models with 4-bit GPTQ/AWQ you can keep weights in ~3-6GB per model. KV is the big driver: each token's KV state scales with hidden size — for a 13B-ish model with 8192 hidden dims, estimate ~1KB per token roundtrip (rough ballpark), so 128k tokens ~128MB — actually wait that's too low, do the math: hidden dim*2 (K+V) * bytes per float/quant * sequence length. With 16-bit that's enormous; with 4-bit quant and packed storage you might be looking at hundreds of MBs to a few GBs depending on architecture. For 70B-class models expect tens of GB of KV for 128k unless you aggressive-quantize and offload.
[03:30] Marcus Lee: So GPUs like A100 80GB could still hold model + hot KV for 128k if quantized aggressively?
[03:36] Priya Menon: Yes for smaller models. For 70B you'd need either GPU sharding across multiple 80GB GPUs or host-offload strategies. We often use a hybrid: shard model across n GPUs and keep active KV for the current conversation on a dedicated KV pool. That lets you keep p95 latency manageable and move cold tokens to host/NVMe.
[03:55] Jordan Blake: To add: our runtime supports per-request routing policies. So you can pin critical users to single-node low-latency pools and route heavy batch jobs to multi-node high-throughput clusters.
[04:06] Samir Patel: What about attention kernels? We've seen FlashAttention gives big wins but fails on very long sequences sometimes. Any recommendations?
[04:13] Priya Menon: FlashAttention is excellent for contiguous sequences; but for huge sequences it's memory-bound. We use a combination: FlashAttention for local windows, and grouped-query or linearized attention for global context—basically a hybrid attention pattern. Another approach is hierarchical attention: compute dense attention in the recent window and a sparse/global attention for far context. Works well with chunking across documents.
[04:37] Elena Rossi: Can you quantify speedups?
[04:40] Priya Menon: On 32k sequences we saw 2-3x lower latency and 40-60% lower memory with Flash+sparsity relative to naive attention. At 128k it's more nuanced—hybrid gives ~3-5x better memory utilization but raw compute still grows; so overall throughput per GPU goes down but cost per useful token can be lower because of smart caching.
[05:00] Marcus Lee: About quantization: GPTQ vs AWQ tradeoffs? We care about output fidelity for clinical summaries.
[05:06] Priya Menon: GPTQ is mature and widely used; AWQ can give better accuracy for some weights but may be slower in decode due to extra dequant steps. Our recommendation: run a small eval with both on your prompt set. For clinical fidelity we usually keep critical heads in higher precision (mixed precision) and quantize the rest. That's called selective or per-layer quantization.
[05:28] Jordan Blake: We'll provide a quant profile template; Priya will share kernel timing so you can see where the extra cycles are.
[05:34] Samir Patel: Networking — if we deploy on-prem in our VPC, do you require access to KMS endpoints? We have an HSM for keys.
[05:41] Jordan Blake: For Private deploy we integrate with customer KMS via TLS and can support HSM endpoints. You control keys. For hosted we offer envelope encryption and can integrate customer-managed keys in many cloud providers.
[05:53] Elena Rossi: Any security caveats when you do offload to host or NVMe?
[05:58] Priya Menon: Yes, encrypted at-rest and in-flight is critical. We encrypt KV pages on NVMe if they're written to disk, and we use mlock/pinned pages for host memory to avoid swapping. Audit logs are generated for every key access. We'll share our SOC2 matrices—Jordan?
[06:12] Jordan Blake: Yep we'll send the security pack including our SOC2 cert and private deployment checklist.
[06:17] [06:17] Samir Patel: There was a note in the RFP about determinism for evaluation. Do inference optimizations change outputs?
[06:22] Priya Menon: Quantization and kernel reorder can slightly change floating point results. For deterministic reproductions we can pin kernels and use deterministic RNGs. However some optimizations (like grouped attention approximations) trade small quality changes for large speedups. We'll highlight delta evaluations so you can choose the sweet spot.
[06:41] Marcus Lee: Let's talk numbers — if we aim for processing a nightly batch of 10k documents average 80k tokens each; what's a plausible throughput?
[06:50] Priya Menon: If you run in high-throughput mode with batching and prefetching, you get amortization. Example rough: On a 4-node cluster (each node A100 80GB, good NVMe, RDMA), assuming chunking to 16k windows and batching 16 windows per step, you could process tens of documents per second aggregate; nightly jobs of that magnitude are plausible. Precise numbers depend on model size, quantization, and overlap factor. We'll run a benchmark with your sample corpus to get real throughput/p95/p99.
[07:19] Samir Patel: Overlap factor—how much redundancy are we incurring when chunking overlapping windows?
[07:24] Priya Menon: Typically 10-20% overlap to maintain context across windows. Hierarchical chunking reduces need for very large overlap by maintaining summaries or embeddings of older chunks. Another trick: store chunk-level embeddings in a vector DB and only bring full tokens for retrieved chunks. That reduces KV pressure.
[07:41] Elena Rossi: Would Redwood's Optimize tool give recommendations on chunk size and quantization?
[07:46] Jordan Blake: Yes, Redwood Optimize analyzes token distributions and suggests batching/quant settings and model variants. It can simulate cost vs quality tradeoffs based on eval prompts.
[07:55] Marcus Lee: We have a constraint: our on-prem nodes are behind an internal firewall with no outbound internet. How does Private deployment work?
[08:01] Priya Menon: Private supports air-gapped deployments. We provide a control plane option that can run as a customer-managed control plane within your VPC. For truly offline, our on-prem install includes an offline installer and offline license activation with signed tokens. The runtime doesn't require external endpoints but we do need a secure channel during initial setup if you want Redwood to manage rollouts.
[08:22] Samir Patel: Great.
[08:24] Priya Menon: A few gotchas for on-prem multi-node: ensure low-latency interconnect (InfiniBand/RDMA) and fast local NVMe for offload. NFS or slow shared storage will kill tail latency because of cold page fetches. Also watch for NUMA balancing; GPUs attached to different CPU sockets can have bandwidth penalties.
[08:43] Marcus Lee: Regarding model rollouts, can we A/B compare quantized vs fp16 models in production?
[08:48] Jordan Blake: Yes, the rollout engine supports canary/A-B with automatic fallback. You can route, for example, 5% traffic to a quantized variant and collect summary metrics and fidelity checks before roll out.
[08:59] Elena Rossi: For evaluation, we need exact logs—kernels, per-token timing, KV hit rates. Can Redwood provide that?
[09:05] Priya Menon: We do. Console exports per-request traces, token-level timing, and KV hit/miss counters. For deeper root cause you'll get per-kernel counters and GPU metrics. Some of that is retained only in Dedicated/Private tiers but we can provide ephemeral logs for the benchmark.
[09:20] Samir Patel: On pricing — if we move to a Dedicated KV pool approach that keeps hot KV on a dedicated set of GPUs, how does billing work?
[09:27] Jordan Blake: Dedicated is capacity-based. You reserve GPU-pools and pay commit pricing. We can model cost scenarios in the spreadsheet we'll send. For hybrid host-offload, there's also storage and IO charges if using Redwood managed NVMe in hosted mode.
[09:40] Marcus Lee: For long-context inference, do you recommend dynamic batching or fixed-step?
[09:45] Priya Menon: Dynamic batching works well when requests arrive with variable lengths. For deterministic nightly jobs we often use fixed-step to maximize throughput. Redwood runtime supports both; we can tune batch flush thresholds based on latency SLOs.
[09:58] Samir Patel: Any specific kernel/library stack recommendations? CUDA version, cuDNN, Triton, FlashAttention versions?
[10:04] Priya Menon: We usually standardize on CUDA 12.x + cuBLAS/cuDNN latest stable, and FlashAttention v2 where supported. For group-query we have custom kernels. For quantized kernels we rely on tensor-core optimized GEMMs; some kernels are upstream (xformers) others are in our runtime tuned for the instance types. We'll share exact matrix.
[10:22] Elena Rossi: For the benchmark, what artifacts do you need from us?
[10:25] Jordan Blake: 1) Sanitized sample corpus (10GB suggested) 2) Typical prompt templates and distribution (how often you call retrieval vs pure summarization) 3) Target SLOs (interactive partials vs bulk windows) 4) Any IP/data residency constraints.
[10:40] Samir Patel: We'll produce that; security team will sanitize.
[10:43] Priya Menon: Great. One more micro-optimization: when you have streaming partials, prefix KV cache warmups can be reduced by reusing chunk encodings — instead of re-encoding identical chunks for each session, we dedupe at the chunk-hash level and maintain a shareable KV for identical chunks. This is especially effective for templated documents.
[11:04] Marcus Lee: That sounds useful.
[11:06] Samir Patel: Any red flags we should be aware of?
[11:09] Priya Menon: Watch for tail latency due to cold KV on NVMe and network hiccups—these are the most common surprises. Also quantization can introduce subtle bias; for clinical output we recommend human-in-the-loop gating for the first months.
[11:23] Jordan Blake: Recap and next steps: Redwood runs hosted benchmark with your corpus, Priya shares kernel timings + quant templates, Jordan sends pricing and benchmark sheet, Nimbus provides sanitized data and target SLOs, schedule on-prem pilot kickoff week of 2025-11-24.
[11:37] Elena Rossi: That works.
[11:39] Samir Patel: Thanks everyone.
[11:41] Jordan Blake: Thanks all — we'll follow up with the artifacts.
[11:44] -- End of recording --
